feature.title: Blacksmiths, broom-makers and a fiddle band at Marble Springs
feature.deck: The governor's farm throws its founder a birthday party once a year, and the whole thing is free. Saturday it turns 281, with working craftspeople on the grounds from eleven to four.

body.text: John Sevier was born in 1745, which makes Saturday his 281st birthday, and the farm he lived on is still standing at the far south end of the county. Marble Springs has thrown him a party every September for years. It costs nothing to walk in, it runs from eleven to four, and the reason to go is the people working: a blacksmith at a live forge, a cook over an open hearth, someone tying a broom by hand, a weaver at a loom, a potter at a wheel.
What's actually happening on the grounds

These are demonstrations, not a museum case — the craftspeople work through the day and will talk while they do it, and the hands-on crafts are open to all ages. It is the rare local event where a nine-year-old and a sixty-year-old get roughly the same thing out of standing at the same table.

body.text: Getting there, and the heat

Marble Springs sits on West Governor John Sevier Highway, past the Urban Wilderness and well south of the Sevier Avenue end of things — it is a drive, not a walk, from the rest of this week's list. Saturday's forecast is mostly sunny and around 94 degrees. A forge on a 94-degree afternoon is exactly as warm as it sounds, so go early, bring water, and plan on the shade being wherever the trees are rather than wherever you are.
One scheduling note worth having: this is the daytime half of a very full Saturday in South Knoxville. The site closes at four, which leaves the evening open.

body.text: A troupe of local and regional performers sets up on the grass outside the Ijams Park Visitor Center on Saturday evening, and for ninety minutes the lawn is a circus: acrobats, aerials and silks, jugglers, and the fire performers the park bills as the reason to stay to the end. The gate and the marketplace open at six; the show starts at 7:30 and runs to nine with an intermission around 8:30.
How the night is built

The hour and a half before the show is the part people underuse. The marketplace is open from six, the food trucks are parked, and the Ijams beer garden is pouring — so the sensible version of Saturday is to arrive at six, eat on the grass, and be settled when the light goes. Sunset is about 7:37, which means the show starts in dusk and finishes in full dark. That is deliberate, and it is why the fire acts are back half.
The practical part

Twenty-two dollars for an adult, fifteen for a kid six to twelve, free under six, and parking is included in the ticket — worth knowing, because parking at Ijams Park otherwise costs five dollars a car. There are no seats: bring a lawn chair or a blanket. And the one conflict to plan around is that Tennessee kicks off at Neyland at 7:45 the same night, fifteen minutes after the circus starts. The two audiences are mostly different people, but the bridges are not.

body.text: Ijams Park and Central Cinema have been running Movies Under the Stars on the Visitor Center lawn since May, and Friday is the big one: Lord of the Rings, outdoors, on a screen, with the actual woods sitting right there behind it. The gate opens at seven and the movie starts when it gets dark, which the park puts at about 8:15.
What to expect on the lawn

Twelve dollars a head, with a discount for Ijams and Central Cinema members. Food trucks and the beer garden handle dinner and drinks — no coolers and no outside alcohol, which the park is direct about. Bring a chair or a blanket. Dogs are allowed and have to be leashed the whole time, and on a Friday night with a crowd that is a rule worth taking seriously.
Two left after this

The series has one more date after Friday — Carrie on October 2, which tells you where the calendar is heading. Buy ahead if you can; the park does not promise walk-up tickets. Friday's forecast is mostly sunny and around 94 with a slight chance of an evening storm, so check the event page before you load the car.

body.text: Tennessee plays Kennesaw State on Saturday at 7:45 on SEC Network — the first night game at Neyland this season, and the last one before conference play starts. None of that is South Knoxville news by itself. What is South Knoxville news is that a 7:45 kickoff moves the whole rhythm of the day: cars start hunting for spaces on this side of the river by mid-afternoon, and the walk back over the bridge happens somewhere around eleven.
Where the spaces actually are

The City counts more than 600 public parking spaces near the Sevier Avenue corridor. More than 200 of those are at Suttree Landing Park and on the streets around it. Another 300-plus are in the Regal garage, which is open to the public on weekends and after six on weekdays. From any of them it is a five-to-ten-minute walk to the Sevier Avenue businesses, and a longer one to the stadium.
If you live here and you are not going

The roundabout construction at Sevier, Foggy Bottom and Island Home is still in the ground, so the corridor is narrower than it looks on a map. Marked pedestrian paths skirt the work. If Saturday night is a stay-home night, it is a good one to walk rather than drive. And if you were planning on the circus at Ijams Park, note that it starts fifteen minutes before kickoff — the lawn is fine, the bridges are the problem.

body.text: Storytime at the Ijams Nature Playscape runs every Saturday morning from ten to noon and costs nothing: somebody reads a book out loud on the blankets, and then it is a craft or it is the climbing logs and the creek. This Saturday the reader is the author. Mona Martin Batchelor will read from "Nora T and the Champion Tree," a children's book of hers that has not been published yet.
Why the Playscape is the right room for it

The Playscape is five acres of deliberately unfinished woods at the Grayson Subaru Preserve — dirt to dig, logs to climb, a creek to stand in. A book about a champion tree read out loud under actual trees is the kind of thing that only works in a place like this, and it is free, which means a family can show up on a whim and leave when the two-year-old is done.
It is a short walk from the Mead's Quarry gravel lot. Saturday will be hot — mostly sunny and around 94 — but the ten-to-noon window is the cool half of that, and the Playscape is shaded.

body.text: Ijams Park runs guided paddles out of its river access on Island Home Pike, and Friday's goes out at six thirty for two hours. Forty-five dollars covers the boat, the paddle and the vest, which is the whole point — it is the version of kayaking available to people who do not have a kayak on the roof of the car.
The timing is the product

Sunset Friday is about 7:39. A six-thirty launch means an hour of low gold light on the way out and dusk on the way back, which is a better trip than the same route at noon in ninety-four-degree heat. The water is flat, the bluffs are wooded on both sides, and the noise of the city drops away faster than you expect for something this close to downtown.
Register ahead — the paddles carry a small number of boats and they sell out. If Friday is full, the same evening has Lord of the Rings on the lawn a few minutes up the road.

body.text: Ijams Park takes small groups into a gated cave on Saturday afternoon, two till four thirty, sixty-five dollars a head. The park's own description is refreshingly free of salesmanship: it calls the trip physically and mentally demanding, and then it lists why.
What they tell you before you sign up

Participants should expect slippery muddy hills, water between knee and thigh deep, and stretches that require crawling and pulling yourself along with your hands and arms. The gated entrance measures about three feet by two. The cave holds around fifty-five degrees all year, which is a forty-degree swing from Saturday's forecast and the single best argument for going.

Registration is required and there are no walk-ins — every participant needs a ticket. There is also a liability waiver, good for the calendar year, so if you have done another Ijams Park program this year you are already covered. Read that list against what your knees are currently willing to do.

body.text: Tennessee's other football team plays Sunday at one. The Titans host Philadelphia at Nissan Stadium on FOX, which is three hours up the interstate and therefore a television game for everyone reading this. Puckers, the sports grill at 115 Mimosa Avenue, runs weekend brunch from nine to two on Saturdays and Sundays with the screens on throughout — so a one o'clock kickoff lands inside the last hour of the brunch menu.
Why this is the odd one out this week

Look at the rest of this weekend and nearly all of it is outdoors and most of it is at Ijams Park. Sunday at Puckers is the alternative: indoors, air-conditioned, and at ninety-three degrees outside that is not a small consideration. The room opened in August in the space that was Mimosas, across the river from the stadium, and brunch survived the change of name.

The Titans are 0–1 after losing to the Jets at home in week one, so this is a Sunday for the faithful rather than a victory party. The Eagles are the better team by a good distance. Parking is in the garage behind the building, which matters more than usual on a weekend when everything on this side of the river is full.

stories.title: Five dollars puts you at the bird-banding table on Sunday morning
stories.deck: Migration is on, and the Ijams Park banding crew lets visitors stand at the table while they work — and hand you the bird to release. It is the cheapest ticket of the weekend.

facts.label: When
facts.value: Sun Sep 20 · 8–9:30 AM

facts.label: Where
facts.value: Meet at the Mead's Quarry lot · 3526 Island Home Ave

facts.label: Cost
facts.value: $5 — and that includes your parking

facts.label: The walk
facts.value: About 500 feet downhill on uneven trail; the table is shaded, with seating

facts.label: Net runs
facts.value: Optional, off-trail — wear long pants and closed shoes

facts.label: Waiver
facts.value: One assumption-of-risk form per calendar year

body.text: The Ijams Park community science team runs its banding station on Sunday morning from eight to nine thirty, and five dollars gets you a place at the table. Trained staff and volunteers catch songbirds in fine mist nets, record the data, fit a numbered leg band, and let them go — and visitors get to see the birds in the hand and release them afterward.
What the station is actually for

The station opened in early 2025 to study how resident and migratory songbirds use fruiting plants through the year, with a particular interest in which birds eat and spread native versus non-native invasive species. The crew bands at sites across the park before and after invasive plant removal to see what changes. All of it runs under a federally authorized banding permit issued by the USGS Bird Banding Laboratory.
The practical part

You meet in the Mead's Quarry gravel lot — there should be a staff member there to point you down — and walk about five hundred feet downhill on uneven trail to the table, which is shaded and has seating. The walk back is short and mostly uphill. Net runs are optional and go off-trail through unmaintained brush and over one small stream, so long pants and real shoes if you want to go along. The five dollars covers parking, so don't pay at the lot.

body.text: Self Care Sunday is an hour of yoga outdoors at Ijams Park with Hope Irwin, eleven thirty to twelve thirty. Ten dollars for anyone thirteen and up, five for children five to thirteen. A parent and two kids comes to twenty dollars for the morning, which is not a sentence you get to write about much of this weekend.
About the heat

It is going to be about ninety-three degrees Sunday and the class is at the warm end of the morning, so this is a water-and-shade situation rather than a gentle-breeze one. Bring your own mat. The upside of an outdoor class in September is the same as it always is — birdsong instead of a speaker, and the walk back to the car through the woods.
It stacks neatly with the rest of Sunday: painting starts at eleven, the mushroom workshop at twelve thirty, and the bluegrass jam at two. You could reasonably do two of the four.

body.text: Paint by the Pond is the September entry in the Ijams Park Creative Series: two hours on Sunday late morning, forty-five dollars, easels set up on the bank of the pond with the water and the treeline as the subject. It is a workshop rather than a class, which in practice means nobody checks whether you can already paint.
Where it sits in the day

Eleven to one on a Sunday is a good slot — the banding crew has packed up, the bluegrass has not started, and the pond is quiet. It is also the hottest part of the day, and the shade on the bank is patchy, so a hat is not optional.
The Creative Series keeps going after this weekend: a hooping workshop on the 24th and stained glass on the 26th. These cap small and are worth booking rather than turning up for.

body.text: The Fall Fungi ID beginner workshop runs Sunday from twelve thirty to two, fifteen dollars, with an Ijams Park naturalist. It is the practical kind of nature program: what a mushroom actually is, which parts have names and which of those names matter, and how to tell a fungus from a lichen at a glance — the confusion that trips up almost everyone at the start.
Why now is the right week

Late September in East Tennessee is when the forest floor starts producing. A fallen log that looked like a fallen log in July is a small city by now. Learning to read one is the sort of thing that permanently changes an ordinary walk, which is a good return on ninety minutes.

This is a repeating series rather than a one-off. If Sunday is full there is another on the 27th at three. Registration is required either way, and the park does not take walk-ins for its education programs.

body.text: The East Tennessee Bluegrass Association and Ijams Park have run a community jam on the third Sunday of the month for a few years now, and this Sunday is the third Sunday. Two to five, free, open to anyone. All skill levels are welcome, which in a jam circle is a real statement rather than a polite one.
The rules, such as they are

Bring any acoustic bluegrass instrument. The one stated exception is harmonicas and spoons, which are not currently part of it. And if you do not play anything at all, come anyway — the association sets chairs out and says so directly. An afternoon of live string-band music for nothing is a decent way to close a weekend.
In colder months the jam moves inside the Visitor Center. In September it is still the good version. More about the association, including how to get on their list, is at ETNBA.org.

body.text: Earl's sits at 610 Waterfront Drive, down where Suttree Landing meets the river, and it runs a different special every day of the week. Thursday is ten-dollar Patrón mango margaritas. Friday is nine-dollar spicy pineapple ones. Saturday is eight-dollar house margaritas, and Sunday is seven-dollar mimosas and Bloody Marys. All of them run the full day, eleven to ten.
The new column

What is new this week is a second Saturday board that runs alongside the margaritas: two dollars off drafts and two off pizza, six-dollar Orange Bliss, and beer buckets at six for the price of five, plus a run of four- and five-dollar shots. It is there because the Vols are home at 7:45, and because the tables at Earl's face open water about ten minutes' walk from where half the stadium crowd parks.

The food is the reason to get there before the drinks are, and eleven in the morning is a real opening time rather than a technicality. If Saturday night belongs to the stadium, Sunday at the water is the recovery.
